questions.q: During a routine cell lysis procedure in a cGMP facility, a technician discovers that extending the designated sonication time by 10 seconds results in a visibly clearer supernatant and potentially higher protein yield. How must the technician proceed regarding the active Standard Operating Procedure (SOP)?
options: Immediately implement the new 10-second extension for all future batches to maximize facility output.
Maintain the currently written SOP times; if an improvement is desired, they must submit a formal request through the facility's Change Control system.
Verbally instruct the rest of the laboratory team to add 10 seconds, but leave the official written SOP unchanged.
Pencil in the new time on the master SOP binder and initial it so operators on the next shift are aware.
questions.explain:
In a regulated cGMP environment, **strict adherence to the approved SOP is an absolute legal requirement**. 

Operators cannot unilaterally change a procedure, even if the change appears to improve the process. Unvalidated changes can have catastrophic downstream effects on drug safety or purity. To legally alter a protocol, the technician must submit a formal proposal to the **Change Control** board, which will require rigorous testing, QA review, and official retraining before the SOP is updated.

questions.q: While executing a validated media preparation SOP, a technician realizes they accidentally incubated a heat-sensitive solution at $37^\circ\text{C}$ for $45 \text{ minutes}$ instead of the explicitly stated $30 \text{ minutes}$. According to strictly regulated laboratory protocols, what is the mandatory immediate action?
options: Record the time as $30 \text{ minutes}$ in the batch record, since $15 \text{ minutes}$ is biologically insignificant for media.
Place the solution in an ice bath for $15 \text{ minutes}$ to mathematically offset the excess heating time.
Document the event as a formal Protocol Deviation, notify a supervisor or Quality Assurance, and quarantine the media until its validity is reviewed.
Discard the current SOP entirely and print a new version from the network drive.
questions.explain:
Any failure to follow an SOP exactly as written is classified as a **Protocol Deviation**. 

The technician must never hide or falsify the mistake (Option 'a') or attempt an unauthorized fix (Option 'b'). Under Good Manufacturing Practices (cGMP), the deviation must be documented exactly as it occurred and flagged for review by the **Quality Assurance (QA)** department, who will determine if the media must be discarded or if the deviation had no material impact on product safety.

questions.q: Biomanufacturing facilities rely extensively on Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for every aspect of production and analysis. What is the fundamental, primary objective of implementing an SOP for a repetitive analytical assay?
options: To ensure absolute consistency, reproducibility, and uniform quality regardless of which trained operator performs the assay.
To entirely eliminate the need for supervisory oversight and basic employee training.
To provide scientists with the underlying theoretical physics equations regarding the assay's mechanism of action.
To act as a flexible set of suggestions that allow technicians to experiment with new chemical ratios.
questions.explain:
The core purpose of a **Standard Operating Procedure (SOP)** is to guarantee **consistency and reproducibility**. 

By providing a highly detailed, step-by-step set of instructions that leaves no room for subjective interpretation, an SOP ensures that whether Technician A performs the assay on Monday or Technician B performs it on Friday, the process is executed identically. SOPs are not flexible suggestions (Option 'd') nor are they theoretical textbooks (Option 'c').
